First off, Opus 5.5 built working weights and code with only two prompts:
1. Read this article and any relevant source code:
https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer
. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.
It returned charts well illustrating any model would be _slow_. But it's still fun, so the second prompt was:
2. I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.
Now while this was an _epic_ run by Opus (5.5 is a crazy capable model), this is a surprisingly well-structured challenge.
There is a long-lived and incredible community of classic gaming emulation work online for it to reference. And that community has created…conformance tests! Opus found them and built against one, that has >3k golden instructions:
https://github.com/christopherpow/nes-test-roms/blob/master/...

With drive letters, a neat functionality in DOS/Windows command prompts (don't ask me about Powershell) is that each letter can have its own "current directory".
So if you have ffmpeg.exe in C:\Program Files\FFMpeg\bin, and you have some source files in D:\SourceVideos, and you want to process them in ffmpeg and output them to E:\Output you can do:
C: (to navigate to the C: drive)
cd "C:\Program Files\FFMpeg\bin"
E: (to navigate to the E:\ drive)
cd D:\SourceVideos (you remain in E:\, but the "current directory" for D: has been changed).
cd Output (to enter E:\Output)
You can now do C:ffmpeg.exe -i D:scene1.mp4 output-scene1.mp4
and Windows accesses the files in the "current" directory on each drive letter.

This is the same style of attack that took 1.5B from Bybit ~1yr ago.
Fundamentally: There is no way to lock webapps to reproducible builds.
Except: IPFS could do it but IPFS has been very very poorly maintained.
I published IPFS-boot ~1yr ago and its a simple idea:
1. deploy a webapp bootloader using something immutable like IPFS
2. bootloader is basically react hot reloading except user agrees what to load
3. bootloader polls a mutable list of app updates and user agree or disagree each update
Now the bootloader has a static content addressable URI but it can also do updates. TBH I think IPFS may be a lost cause but something needs to take its place and this idea is transferable to whatever that is.
